hypothesis: Across regional floras, the naturalised alien flora adds a larger proportion of new genera (relative to native genera) than new species (relative to native species), i.e. a substantial share of naturalised species belong to genera absent from the native flora.
pass_criterion: For regions with matched native checklists (n>=20 regions), the median ratio R = (alien-only genera / native genera) / (alien species / native species) exceeds 1.0, with a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on log(R) at p<0.01, and at least 60% of regions have R>1. Alien-only genus = genus with at least one naturalised species in the region and no native species there.
fail_criterion: Median R <= 1.0, or the Wilcoxon test gives p>=0.05 in the direction R>1, or fewer than 50% of regions have R>1.
interpretation: Darwin's 'flora' is a regional flora, with its 'natives' being the native species and genera of the region. 'Naturalisation' maps to GloNAF's status of a taxon as naturalised in a region. 'Gain proportionally' is each gain divided by the native total: new genera / native genera against new species / native species, which is the ratio R. Darwin's native counts come from his own sources, so a modern native checklist for each region (e.g. from WCVP or POWO distributions) must be joined to GloNAF. Taxonomy is harmonised to current WCVP names, so genus boundaries differ from Darwin's. The claim is tested for all floras and not just for the regions Darwin had in mind (e.g. the US, Europe and New Zealand).

dataset.name: GloNAF – Global Naturalized Alien Flora
dataset.publisher: GloNAF consortium (van Kleunen, Pyšek, Dawson, Essl, Weigelt et al.); data on Zenodo
dataset.why_it_fits: GloNAF v2.0 lists 16,429 naturalised plant taxa across 1,343 regions, with names harmonised to WCVP. Fields to use: region, taxon name, genus, and naturalisation status. Native species and genus counts per region come from a joined native checklist (WCVP/POWO), so alien-only genera and alien species counts can be compared with the native totals.
